strengths: Identifies and formalizes a timely, underexplored incentive problem (moral hazard in pay-per-token LLM pricing due to non-unique tokenization), framed cleanly as a principal-agent model.

Provides a full theoretical arc: (1) shows pay-per-token rewards maximal-length tokenizations, (2) proves NP-hardness of finding the longest *plausible* tokenization under top-p sampling via an elegant reduction from Hamiltonian path, with extensions to top-k sampling and probability-threshold plausibility criteria, (3) gives a clean full characterization theorem showing incentive-compatible additive mechanisms must price linearly in character counts, uniquely identifying pay-per-character.

Backs the theory with a concrete, efficient heuristic algorithm (with stated complexity) and empirical validation across five open-weight LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) and 400 real-world prompts, showing measurable overcharging (up to ~13%) and reporting confidence intervals across repeated runs.

Proposes a practical, easy-to-adopt fix (pay-per-character) along with a concrete transition/calibration scheme (rc = r0/cpt) to avoid revenue disruption, and highlights the positive side-effect of incentivizing shorter/more efficient tokenizations.

Reasonably thorough limitations/discussion section that is honest about scope (additive mechanisms only, single-evaluation cost assumption, use of open rather than proprietary models, LMSYS prompt representativeness) and broader impact considerations regarding dual-use of the heuristic.
weaknesses: The headline 'attack' in Section 3.1 (reporting every character as a separate token, yielding ~300% overcharge) is an almost trivial, obviously-detectable strategy that the paper itself concedes would 'raise suspicion'; its inclusion inflates the apparent severity of the problem without much insight, and the real contribution (Algorithm 1) yields much more modest gains (up to ~13%, and only at temperature >1.0), suggesting the practical financial incentive under realistic settings is fairly small.

The threat model assumes users cannot detect misreporting without provider-supplied next-token distributions, but in practice users do observe the raw output text and (in some APIs) token boundaries; a moderately attentive user might already flag implausible fragmentations (e.g., single-character token runs) without needing formal transparency guarantees, which somewhat undercuts the motivation for the elaborate plausibility/hardness analysis.

The transparency requirement underlying the hardness result (sharing next-token distributions) is explicitly acknowledged as something providers are 'highly reluctant' to do, which limits the real-world applicability of contributions 2 and 3 to a hypothetical regulatory regime rather than current practice.

The cost model (linear in token count, ignoring prefill/prompt-processing costs, batching, hardware utilization effects) is a strong simplification that may not hold precisely in production systems, potentially affecting the realism of the incentive analysis.

Experiments are limited to small-to-medium open-weight models (1B-8B parameters) and a filtered 400-prompt subset of LMSYS chat data with length restrictions (20-100 chars) and English-only, raising questions about generalizability to the large proprietary frontier models that dominate commercial LLM-as-a-service (a limitation the authors do note but do not empirically address).

The paper does not empirically or theoretically explore whether the proposed pay-per-character mechanism introduces new gaming vectors (e.g., unnecessary verbosity, padding with low-cost characters, or degraded output quality to save generation cost while other pricing dimensions remain unmonitored), leaving the incentive-compatibility claim narrowly scoped to tokenization misreporting alone rather than to overall provider honesty.

strengths: Novel and timely framing of pay-per-token pricing as a principal-agent/moral-hazard problem distinct from prior work on LLM-as-a-service economics (e.g., Cai et al., Saig et al.), which focus on model substitution rather than tokenization misreporting.

The NP-hardness result (Theorem 3), via a clean reduction from Hamiltonian path, is a rigorous and non-trivial technical contribution that formally grounds the claim that optimal undetectable misreporting is computationally hard, with sensible extensions to top-k sampling and probability-threshold plausibility criteria (Appendix B.1.1-B.1.2).

The characterization of incentive-compatible additive pricing mechanisms (Theorem 6) is elegant and provides a principled derivation of the pay-per-character mechanism as essentially the unique fair alternative, going beyond an ad hoc proposal.

The paper backs its theoretical claims with a concrete, efficient heuristic algorithm (Algorithm 1) and empirical validation across multiple open-weight model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) and real-world-derived prompts (LMSYS Chatbot Arena), giving the abstract argument some practical teeth.
Limitations and broader impact are discussed candidly, including the dual-use nature of the heuristic algorithm and the restriction to additive mechanisms.
weaknesses: The threat model's practical relevance is questionable: for most commonly used tokenizers (e.g., BPE with deterministic greedy merges), a user with access to the (often public) tokenizer could independently re-encode the returned string and check the token count against what is billed, without needing the provider to reveal next-token probabilities. The paper does not adequately address why this simpler form of auditing would not already curb the described exploit, undermining the motivation for the more elaborate transparency-based analysis.

The heuristic algorithm's meaningful overcharging gains (~9-13%) are only demonstrated at atypically high sampling temperatures (1.3-1.45), which are uncommon defaults in production APIs (typically ~0.7-1.0); at more realistic temperatures the method is shown to be largely ineffective, substantially limiting the real-world significance of the empirical results.

All experiments use small-to-medium open-weight models (1B-8B parameters) rather than the proprietary, commercial frontier models (e.g., GPT, Gemini, Claude) that actually operate under pay-per-token billing in practice; it is unclear whether the findings transfer to the systems the paper's motivation is centered on.

The proposed pay-per-character mechanism is not critically examined for its own fairness/incentive issues: prior cited work (Petrov et al.) shows per-character/per-byte accounting can disadvantage certain languages or scripts (e.g., CJK vs. Latin), and a switch to character-based pricing could reintroduce cross-lingual inequities or encourage providers to trade off output quality/completeness for brevity—neither issue is analyzed despite being directly relevant to the paper's central proposal.

The headline ~3x overcharge figure (Table 1, reporting each character as a separate token) is an extreme, trivially detectable case that the paper itself acknowledges is implausible under any realistic transparency requirement, making it more of a rhetorical device than a substantive empirical finding; the more defensible ~13% figure from Algorithm 1 is comparatively modest.

The NP-hardness result, while technically sound, has limited practical bite since the paper's own heuristic largely circumvents the hardness barrier in a majority of tested settings (for p=0.99), somewhat undercutting the narrative that transparency requirements meaningfully protect users.

Experimental scale is modest (400 prompts, single-seed generation repeated 5 times) and confidence intervals in Table 1 for the trivial character-splitting baseline are unnecessary given its deterministic/certain outcome, suggesting some looseness in reporting rigor.

strengths: Identifies a novel, timely, and practically relevant problem: the moral-hazard incentive created by pay-per-token pricing in LLM-as-a-service, framed rigorously as a principal-agent problem.

Strong theoretical contributions: (1) a clean proof that pay-per-token incentivizes maximal splitting of output into single-character tokens, (2) an NP-hardness result (via reduction from Hamiltonian path) showing that finding the longest *plausible* tokenization under top-p/top-k sampling is computationally hard, with careful extensions to top-k sampling and probability-threshold plausibility in the appendix, and (3) a full characterization theorem showing that incentive-compatible additive pricing mechanisms must be linear in character counts, yielding a uniquely determined pay-per-character mechanism.

The proof-of-concept heuristic (Algorithm 1) is simple, efficient (near-linear complexity), and empirically demonstrated to meaningfully overcharge users (up to ~13%) across multiple open-weight model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral), lending credibility to the theoretical hardness/heuristic-feasibility gap.

The proposed pay-per-character mechanism is not just theoretically motivated but accompanied by a practical, low-friction transition strategy (normalizing price by empirical characters-per-token) and a discussion of positive downstream incentives (shorter, more efficient tokenizations) that it creates for honest providers.

Reasonably thorough experimental section and appendix (multiple temperatures, models, illustrative token-split examples, licensing/reproducibility details) that support and illustrate the theoretical claims.
Honest and specific limitations/broader impact discussion, including appropriate caveats about the heuristic being a proof-of-concept rather than a deployable attack.
weaknesses: The empirically demonstrated overcharging via Algorithm 1 is largely confined to high-temperature regimes (>1.0), which are not the default/most common operating point for most API usage (e.g., factual QA, coding); the practical severity of the vulnerability under typical default settings (e.g., temperature ~0.7-1.0) is not clearly established.

The scenario in which the heuristic is applicable presumes providers already publish next-token distributions/logprobs for every generated token, which is not standard practice among major commercial API providers today; the practical relevance of the demonstrated attack to real-world deployments is therefore somewhat limited and could be discussed more explicitly.

All experiments use open-weight models as stand-ins for provider behavior; there is no evaluation (or even indirect evidence) involving actual commercial API providers, so the headline claim in the title ("Is your LLM overcharging you?") is not directly tested against real deployed pricing/tokenization practices.

The proposed pay-per-character mechanism, while provably incentive-compatible in this model, could introduce new fairness/value-misalignment concerns (e.g., different languages/scripts require different numbers of characters to convey equivalent content, as noted by cited work on tokenizer unfairness across languages) that are not analyzed, despite being a natural extension of the paper's own incentive-compatibility framework.

The threat model is restricted to tokenization misreporting; other easier and arguably more impactful provider strategies (e.g., generating unnecessarily verbose content, or, as discussed by cited related work, silently substituting a cheaper model) are excluded by design, which somewhat narrows the practical significance of the specific mechanism studied, though this is acknowledged as a limitation.

The linear generation-cost assumption c(t) = c0·len(t) is a simplification of real-world serving costs (e.g., batching effects, KV-cache reuse, quadratic attention costs at scale) that could affect the tightness of the incentive-compatibility argument, though the choice is reasonably justified by cited energy-scaling studies.

strengths: Novel and timely framing of tokenization ambiguity as a principal-agent/moral hazard problem in LLM-as-a-service pricing, an angle that appears underexplored relative to prior work on model-substitution or reasoning-token injection.

Solid theoretical contributions: a clean proof that finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p (and top-k, and probability-threshold) sampling is NP-hard via a well-constructed reduction from Hamiltonian path; a clear characterization theorem showing that additive incentive-compatible pricing must be linear in character counts, with the pay-per-character mechanism as the natural instantiation.

The heuristic overcharging algorithm (Algorithm 2) is simple, well-motivated by empirical plausibility patterns, and the paper goes the extra mile to show it is financially profitable net of verification costs, using real GPU energy measurements rather than just token counts.

Broad and careful empirical validation across three model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral), multiple temperatures, top-p thresholds, and margin levels, with confidence intervals and consistent trends across appendix ablations.
The practical prescription for providers to preserve average profit margin when switching to pay-per-character is a nice, actionable bridge between theory and deployment.

Thoughtful limitations/broader-impact section: acknowledges dual-use risk of the algorithm, discusses market-level effects not modeled, notes verbosity-gaming as an unresolved issue even under pay-per-character, and flags dataset/model representativeness concerns.
Reasonable reproducibility: detailed experimental setup (hardware, prompts, generation settings, licenses) and a code repository reference.
weaknesses: The empirical demonstration of significant overcharging relies heavily on unusually high sampling temperatures (1.3–1.45), which are atypical for most production LLM-as-a-service defaults (often ≤1.0); at temperature 1.15 or lower, effects appear much smaller (per appendix figures), so the headline overcharging percentages may overstate real-world exposure.

The main mitigation pathway (requiring providers to reveal next-token distributions) is itself acknowledged as unlikely to be adopted by proprietary providers, and the paper does not propose or evaluate a concrete verification protocol (e.g., via trusted execution environments or cryptographic commitments) that would make the 'transparency' remedy practically enforceable; this is left as future work, limiting the immediate practical impact of the hardness result.

Even the proposed incentive-compatible pay-per-character mechanism does not close the loop: providers could still misreport the tokenizer, inflate verbosity, or misreport next-token distributions, all acknowledged but not analyzed quantitatively, leaving open how much of the original moral-hazard problem is actually solved end-to-end.

Experiments are restricted to small open-weight models (1B–8B parameters); the paper does not test on larger or proprietary frontier models where actual commercial pricing and stakes are highest, which is a nontrivial external validity gap given the paper's motivating claim about cloud LLM services.

The analysis is confined to a single user-single provider micro-economic setting; competitive/market dynamics, reputational effects, and repeated-interaction auditing (which could substantially change incentives) are explicitly out of scope, somewhat narrowing the practical significance of the incentive-compatibility results.

The value function v(t)=v(str(t)) assumption, while reasonable, glosses over subtleties (e.g., latency/streaming effects of many small tokens, or user-side heuristics for estimating expected token counts from text) that could affect how 'undetectable' overcharging really is in practice.

strengths: Original and timely framing: models the interaction between LLM-as-a-service providers and users as a principal-agent problem with moral hazard arising from non-unique tokenization, an angle that has not been systematically studied before.

Solid theoretical contributions: a clean NP-hardness proof (via reduction from Hamiltonian path) for finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p sampling, with sensible extensions to top-k sampling and probability-threshold plausibility criteria.

A crisp and elegant characterization theorem showing that additive incentive-compatible pricing mechanisms must be linear in character counts, which cleanly motivates the proposed pay-per-character alternative.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation across three model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) and real prompts (LMSYS Chatbot Arena), including energy-cost measurements to justify the assumption that verification cost is independent of sequence length and that misreporting can be profitable net of costs.

Practical prescription for margin-preserving transition from pay-per-token to pay-per-character, plus a fairness observation that pay-per-character could reduce the extra cost multilingual/non-English users currently face.

Honest and fairly comprehensive limitations section, acknowledging that pay-per-character does not prevent verbosity inflation and that the analysis is restricted to a single user-provider dyad rather than market-level dynamics.
weaknesses: The core threat model (Section 3) presupposes providers voluntarily disclose next-token distributions/top-p parameters to enable 'plausibility' checks; real commercial APIs do not expose this information, so it is unclear the hardness results or Algorithm 2's suspicion-avoidance mechanism have any bearing on actual deployed systems where users have no way to check plausibility at all.

The empirically demonstrated overcharging is modest and appears concentrated at atypically high temperatures (1.3–1.45) rarely used in production defaults (~0.7–1.0); results in Appendix C.1 suggest the effect shrinks substantially at temperature 1.15, raising doubts about real-world magnitude and significance of the vulnerability under typical serving conditions.

The proposed fix (pay-per-character) does not close the fundamental incentive problem: providers can still inflate revenue by increasing verbosity of the underlying string itself, a loophole the authors acknowledge but do not analyze quantitatively, undermining the practical value of the main proposed remedy.

A simpler and arguably more direct fix — requiring a canonical/deterministic tokenizer or verifiable tokenization procedure (briefly mentioned via related work on canonical autoregressive generation) — is not seriously discussed or compared against pay-per-character, leaving open whether changing the pricing unit is actually the best solution relative to enforcing tokenization determinism.

Cost modeling is stylized (energy cost linear in length, verification cost constant regardless of length) and ignores other real provider costs (engineering/legal/reputational risk of being caught misreporting), which are exactly the kinds of costs that would dominate a rational provider's decision to strategize in practice; the 'financial viability' argument is therefore incomplete.

Experiments are limited to small-to-mid-size open-weight models (1B–8B parameters) and a few hundred prompts from a single (criticized) benchmark; it is unclear how findings transfer to the large proprietary frontier models that dominate real LLM-as-a-service markets, which the paper itself flags as future work rather than addressing.

The incentive-compatibility results, while clean, are relatively straightforward consequences of the additive-pricing definitions once the model is set up, and the overall contribution feels narrower than the framing suggests once the transparency assumption and verbosity loophole are taken into account.

strengths: The paper formalizes a novel and practically relevant problem—tokenization misreporting under pay-per-token LLM pricing—using a clean principal-agent framework, clearly identifying the moral hazard created by information asymmetry between providers and users.

The theoretical contributions are well-developed and rigorous: Theorem 3 (NP-hardness of finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p sampling, with extensions to top-k sampling and probability-threshold plausibility) is proven via a non-trivial reduction from the Hamiltonian path problem, and Theorem 6 (characterization of incentive-compatible pricing mechanisms as linear in character count) is elegant and has strong practical implications.

The proof-of-concept heuristic (Algorithm 2) is a nice complement to the hardness result, showing that even though optimal undetectable misreporting is intractable, a simple and cheap heuristic can still yield meaningful, financially profitable overcharging in practice, which strengthens the paper's real-world relevance.

Experiments are reasonably thorough: multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) and sizes, multiple temperature/p settings, energy-cost measurements to justify the cost model, and a language-stratified analysis of the pay-per-character transition (Figure 12) that reveals an interesting fairness angle for underrepresented languages.
The proposed pay-per-character prescription for maintaining average profit margins during a transition from pay-per-token is simple, actionable, and empirically validated.

The limitations section is candid and thorough, acknowledging model assumptions, the narrow micro-level scope, dependence on LMSYS prompts, and alternative provider misbehaviors not addressed by pay-per-character (e.g., increasing verbosity).
weaknesses: The empirical overcharging magnitudes shown by Algorithm 2 are quite modest for realistic p values (e.g., ~1.8% at p=0.95, ~0.28% at p=0.9 for Llama-3.2-1B), and mainly become large only at p=0.99 or high temperatures (>1.0) atypical of most production use (e.g., factual/coding queries), which somewhat undercuts the paper's framing of "significant" overcharging as a pressing real-world threat.

The verification cost model (constant cv independent of sequence length) is derived from a specific measurement setup and may not generalize to all serving stacks (e.g., different batching, quantization, or hardware), and the financial viability analysis in Eq. 4 relies on this assumption without broader robustness checks across serving configurations.

The pay-per-character solution does not address several practical attack vectors acknowledged by the authors themselves (e.g., inflating verbosity, misreporting next-token distributions, or shipping a public tokenizer different from the internal one), leaving open significant avenues by which an unfaithful provider could still exploit users, which somewhat limits the completeness of the proposed remedy.

The experiments rely exclusively on relatively small open-weight models (1B-8B parameters) and cannot directly speak to proprietary frontier LLM APIs (GPT, Gemini, Claude) where the phenomenon is most economically consequential, since those systems' tokenizers, sampling settings, and internal reporting practices are inaccessible to external researchers.

The paper's analysis is confined to a single user-single provider micro-level interaction, as acknowledged, and does not model competitive or reputational effects that might already discipline providers in practice, so the practical urgency of regulatory intervention is not fully substantiated.
